## Ch. 8 — A hundred lines instead of twenty

The short messages were six to twenty-two lines. What comes next runs to more than a hundred, across several rock surfaces at a time.[^45] These are the major rock edicts, and they are a different instrument: longer, more elaborate, and mixing personal material with political practice at a length nobody had attempted.

They are at Erragudi in Andhra, Girnar in Gujarat, Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in north-west Pakistan, Kandahar, Kalsi in Uttarakhand, and at Dhauli and Jaugada in Orissa.[^46] Some have not lasted. Sopara in Maharashtra has fragments of three. Sannathi in Karnataka has four.

The career he lays out in them has dates on it. Kalinga around 261/260 BCE, in his eighth year, and it is the only conquest mentioned anywhere in the whole corpus.[^47] Then the tenth year, a pilgrimage to Mahabodhi, and the start of what he calls the second part of his reign.

**And the touring changed name and purpose**. A *vihara yatra* was a royal pleasure tour, and hunting was what it was for.[^48] The *Mahabharata* has one, and the invitation reads: this also is an excellent season for thy son to go a-hunting. What he did instead were *dhamma yatras* — visiting Shramanas and Brahmanas and making gifts, visiting the aged and supporting them with gold, visiting the people of the country.

By 257/256 BCE the officials were carrying it too. The *rajukkas* and *pradeshikas* were ordered to add an inspection circuit every five years, on top of their ordinary duties, and preach.[^49] The content is four lines and every clause is a plain one:

> Meritorious is obedience to mother and father. Meritorious is liberality to friends, acquaintances and relatives and to Shramanas and Brahmanas. Meritorious is abstention from the slaughter of living beings. Meritorious is to spend little (and) to store little.

There is a deviation in that list worth having. *Shramanas* are ascetic renunciants, including but not limited to Buddhist monks.[^50] He names Brahmanas alongside them, every time, in a formula he keeps repeating.

In his twelfth year he announced that it had worked. For many hundreds of years slaughter of lives, cruelty to living creatures, and disrespect to relatives and to Shramanas and Brahmanas had increased.[^51] Now the reverse had increased, to a degree not achievable for many hundreds of years in the past. **Whether anybody believed him is the chapter's own question, and it answers it with a comparison**. Modern governments with far better communications and far more effective coercion have not managed simultaneous social transformation across the regions of India.

Then he tried to bolt it to the future. His sons, grandsons and great-grandsons will promote this practice of Dharma till the time of universal destruction.[^52] It became a standard formula in later inscriptions and he is the first to use it. To listeners in the third century BCE, familiar with sons who murdered fathers for thrones, it must have sounded like exactly what it was.

In the thirteenth year he built an institution for it. A new and very senior class of officials, the *dharma-mahamatras*, spread across his dominions.[^53] Their brief was to work out, among the adherents of Dharma, whether a person is only inclined towards Dharma, or is fully established in it, or is merely given to charity.

**And he made himself permanently interruptible**. Formerly there was no transaction of state business and no reporting at all hours. So he made an arrangement:[^54]

> The reporters should report to me the affairs of the people at any time and place, whether I am engaged in eating (or) am in the harem (or) in the bed-chamber (or) on a promenade (or) in a carriage (or) on the march.

The *Arthashastra* had wanted that too, and the difference is where it happens. The manual has the king always active, hearing urgent matters, never putting them off — and it designates places for public interaction, with audiences held in the assembly hall.[^55] The manual's other line runs even closer: in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king, and what is dear to himself is not beneficial to the king, but what is dear to the subjects is. The likeliest reading is not coincidence. A ruler in Pataliputra was very unlikely not to know that work at least by repute.

How the anthology got onto the rocks varies from place to place, and the variation is visible in the letter sizes. At Kalsi one part of a fine-grained rock was polished and the first nine edicts cut into it in very small letters, with the rest below in different lettering.[^56] Shahbazgarhi used more than one rock and Kharoshthi rather than Brahmi: the first eleven on the east face up a hill, the next on a separate boulder at the foot, and the last two on the west face. Mansehra copies that pattern.

Girnar is the exception and it looks like one. Thirty metres of a granite boulder carries all fourteen, in uniform writing, in neat columns, each edict divided from the next by straight lines with the compartments still clearly visible.[^57] **That is a single order carried out at once, by somebody who had the whole set in hand**.

At Erragudi he is called a king for the first time, added to the old title.[^58] And this king opens not with what he has built but with what he wants stopped:

> Here no living being should be slaughtered for sacrifice. And also no festive gathering should be held. For the Beloved of the Gods sees manifold evil in festive gatherings.

**That lands in a world where killing animals for the gods was how the gods were fed**. The megaliths of the Karnataka–Andhra belt put animal parts in with the human dead. In Hindu practice goats, oxen, rams and horses were common offerings, and the *Mahabharata* says animals killed in sacrifice with Vedic mantras went to heaven.[^59]

He knew it would sting, which is probably why the prohibition comes with his own kitchen attached. Many hundred thousands of living beings were formerly slaughtered every day in the king's kitchen for the sake of curry, and now, as this record is written, only three creatures are killed.[^60]

The rhetoric is built for the ear. Where war drums had sounded he was now sounding morality — *bherighoso aho dhammaghoso*, the drum of battle become the drum of dhamma.[^61] And "formerly, in the ages gone by" comes round and round through the edicts for effect.

The seventh edict wants all religious sects to live everywhere in his dominions. The twelfth goes much further, and it is not a request for people to leave each other alone:[^62]

> restraint in regard to speech, (which means) that there should be no extolment of one's own sect or disparagement of other sects on inappropriate occasions… Truly, if (a person) extols his own sect and disparages other sects with a view to glorifying his own sect owing merely to his attachment (to it, he) injures his own sect very severely by acting in that way.

**Praising your own religion loudly is described as damage to your own religion**. The tolerance being asked for is not cordial disregard. It is active concord, and he backs it with gifts and honours to men of all religious communities, ascetics and householders alike — given, he says, so that dhamma may grow among them.[^63]

The same anthology is far less patient about ceremonies. The ninth edict lists the rites he thinks superficial: the auspicious ceremony at an illness, at a wedding, at a birth.[^64] Which is a man telling people how to run the days of their own lives, and it sits a few boulders from the plea for tolerance.

The thirteenth is where he finally writes Kalinga down, and then does something else with it. He lists who has been conquered by dhamma instead — the Yavana king Antiyoka six hundred *yojanas* away, and beyond him Tulamaya, Antikeni, Maka and Alikasudara, and southwards the Cholas and Pandyas.[^65] Those were powerful independent rulers. **Announcing your sway over people you have not fought is still announcing your sway**, and some of them were states an expanding Mauryan empire had had designs on.

The limits get stated in the same edict, which is the honest part of it. The forest peoples are told plainly that pacification has not been ruled out.[^66] The *Arthashastra* is blunt about why: the Atavika, living in their own territory, are many and brave, fight openly, and seize and ruin. And the instruction to his successors is written for men he expects to disobey it — he asks that they not think of fresh conquests, and then, accepting that they will, asks that if they do conquer they take pleasure in patience and light punishment.

He even explains why some versions are long. Some topics have been repeated over and over again owing to their sweetness, so that people may act accordingly.[^67]

**And the last point of the chapter is about what he did not do**. Kings coined themselves — the Indo-Greek rulers put their names on coins in Greek and Prakrit. Others had themselves sculpted; the Kushanas were fond of it.[^68] There is no imperial portrait of Ashoka on a coin or in stone, and no courtly structure anybody can point to. The artefact that is indisputably his is the epigraph, and the empire has to be seen through those.

## Ch. 9 — The same words, four different places

A British army antiquarian looks at Girnar before anybody can read it. James Tod called it the noblest monument of Saurashtra, speaking in an unknown tongue of other times — a huge hemispherical mass of dark granite protruding through the crust of mother earth like a wart, without fissure or inequality, which by the aid of the iron pen **had been converted into a book**.[^69]

He could not read a word of it and he had the shape of the thing exactly right. It is monument and inscription at once, an ancient rock made into a monument by the writing put on it.

The layout there had a practical consequence. All fourteen edicts on one compact face means an official on a platform could stand at eye level with them and read down to a crowd below.[^70] At Erragudi that is impossible — the edicts are spread across boulders at different heights, so nobody could have read the set aloud in one go.

What was around that rock is known only because somebody wrote it down 350 years later. Rudradaman's inscription records that the dam at Junagadh was built by Vaisya Pushyagupta, a provincial governor of Chandragupta, and that conduits were added to it by the Yavana king Tushaspha, who governed the province under Ashoka.[^71] **One of Ashoka's provincial governors shared his ethnicity with the Yavana rulers on the empire's north-western border**, and no Mauryan record says so.

The dam was found in the nineteenth century by a local official. Khan Bahadur Ardeseer Jamsedjee, Naib Diwan of the princely state, traced blocks of masonry running across the river from the north bank to the easternmost spur of the Uparkot rocks, with a breach thirty-six yards long.[^72] The lake behind it would have covered some 140 acres. In the Dharagir garden he found labourers digging out huge stone blocks forming a hollow pavement running north from the bank — the remains, most likely, of the conduits Rudradaman credits to Ashoka.

Why the water mattered is a matter of geology rather than piety. Wells in city areas have to go very deep, and the medieval *vavas* at Junagadh do — the Adi-Chadi Vava drops forty-one metres.[^73] **Wells that deep were not dug in Mauryan times**. Taxila is the parallel: the Bhir plateau stood too high to dig for water, so the city drank from a rivulet outside it. A dam and a lake are what a Mauryan administration could actually build.

And Girnar is missing something the poorer sites have. The whole set is there and the personal Buddhist declaration is not.[^74] The chapter's answer is that it did not need the rock space, because the landscape already said it. The Bhoria stupa stands on a knoll seven kilometres east of the city, a solid brick structure like the Mauryan stupas at Vaishali and Sarnath, and it gave up relic boxes of copper, silver and gold.

Large burnt brick keeps turning up around those hills — at Surajkund, in the Hasnapur dam area, at other spots in the forest.[^75] Put the sites on the topography and they begin to make sense as a circuit. **Girnar was a Buddhist landscape long before it was famous as a Jaina and Hindu one**, and the provincial capital would have been what supported the circuit.

Sannathi in Karnataka shows the reverse problem — a message whose place is lost. The edicts there are on a free-standing slab inscribed on both sides, and it was not found where it stood.[^76] It turned up serving as the pedestal of the idol of Kalikamba in the Chandralamba temple.

Two of the edicts on it had been known only from Dhauli and Jaugada in Orissa, which had made them look like something written specially for Kalinga.[^77] They were not. And the big habitational mound at Sannathi is named Ranamandala, which suggests a battlefield — on which somebody has built a case that the Mauryas conquered the region here. **Nothing in the emperor's own message anywhere refers to any such conquest**, which the chapter says is not enough evidence.

Orissa is where the editing is clearest, because the edicts there survive well. Three of the fourteen were left out at Dhauli and Jaugada: number 11, restating his idea of dhamma; number 12, the great statement on tolerance; and number 13, the account of the Kalinga conquest in full detail.[^78] Two new ones were put in instead.

The omission of the Kalinga edict in Kalinga is the one that explains itself. Only a few years had passed, and he was not going to rub salt into those wounds.[^79] At Dhauli they made a monument of it: a space specially cut for the edicts, and above them, on a terrace, an elephant hewn out of the solid rock.

The Separate Edicts speak to the officials at Tosali and Samapa by name, and they open with a sentence that is not about religion at all.[^80]

> All men are my children. As on behalf of (my own) children I desire that they may be provided by me with all welfare and happiness in this world and in the other world, even so is my desire for all men.

The officials are told to make people learn that the king is to them like a father. **And the chapter puts the obvious question: why here?** Nobody in Gujarat or the north-west was told this.[^81] The likeliest reason is that a newly conquered people were being handled roughly by Mauryan officials, and he knew it.

The borderers get the same treatment and a franker admission underneath it. It might occur to my unconquered borderers to ask what the king desires with reference to us.[^82] The answer: that they may not be afraid of me, but may have confidence in me; that they may obtain only happiness from me, not misery; that the king will forgive them what can be forgiven. **People who had just watched him go through Kalinga had every reason to think they were next**, and the edict is a man arguing against his own reputation.

Then the practical part, which is about judges. The passage is worth having whole, because it describes a specific failure rather than a virtue:[^83]

> It happens in the administration (of justice) that a single person suffers either imprisonment or harsh treatment. In this case (an order) cancelling the imprisonment is obtained by him accidentally, while (many) other people continue to suffer. In this case you must strive to deal (with all of them) impartially.

And then the list of what stops an official doing that: **envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness, and fatigue**. The root of all of it, he says, is the absence of anger and the avoidance of hurry. A man fatigued in the administration of justice will not rise, and one ought to move, to walk, and to advance.

The consequences are put in the only currency that reaches an official. Fail and there is neither attainment of heaven nor satisfaction of the king.[^84] Do it and they discharge the debt he owes — the debt to living beings he had claimed as his own in the Sixth Edict, now handed to the men who actually decide cases.

He also fixed the reading schedule and set a supervisor over it. The edict must be listened to on every day of the constellation Tishya, and by individuals on other occasions in between.[^85] Every five years a *mahamatra* of suitable character — neither harsh nor fierce, but of gentle actions — was to come and check whether the judicial officers had done what they were told. The same scrutiny was ordered at Ujjayini and at Takshashila.

**So the parts of the anthology that landed in the province he had wrecked are not about dhamma at all**. They are about running a court properly in a politically dangerous place.[^86] The message changes with the ground it is standing on, and the chapter's whole point is that the fixity of stone makes it look as though it never did.

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## Ch. 6 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and the empire was already using it**. The Mahasthangarh and Sohgaura plaques show the working method for reaching officials: a portable inscribed plaque, addressed to *mahamatras*, carrying an instruction about grain in famine. That is administration, and it stays inside the administration. The whole existing machinery of palm leaf and birch bark was built for exactly that.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the post-Kalinga message had gone out that way — perishable, to officials, unpublished. He keeps the policy and loses the audience. The forecast is that dhamma becomes a directive rather than a confession, the *rajukkas* enforce it as they enforce everything else, and it dies with the dynasty because nothing carries it. What actually makes the difference is not the sentiment but the surface: **birch bark survived at exactly one site in India, and only because it burned**. He picked the medium that outlasts the state that issues it, and nobody had done that with a personal statement before.

## Ch. 7 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the Kandahar rock, where the Greek says the king abstains from killing and the Aramaic says that for the feeding of our Lord the king, little is killed.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would find the emperor on the wrong side of his own line. What a man eats is inside his power. What a translator three thousand kilometres away writes on a rock is not. Issuing an absolute claim about your own conduct into a language you cannot read is handing the strongest thing you have — the truth of the statement — to a stranger.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]]** reads the same rock as competent rather than careless. Two texts, one stone, and the softer version sits in the language of the working administration. That is how an empire says an absolute thing in the capital's voice and a survivable thing in the province's. Whether he intended it or not, the effect is that nobody in Kandahar had to be caught out.

**They split, and the split is the useful part**. One says the discrepancy is the cost of governing what you cannot inspect. The other says it is the mechanism by which governing at that distance is possible at all. The book does not choose between them either, and says outright that it does not know whether an exemplar came from the king or the translators were left free.

## Ch. 8 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: making a rule apply to yourself first, in public, before you impose it**.

The kitchen line is the mechanism. He bans killing animals for sacrifice — in a world where that is how gods get fed — and in the same edict publishes the count from his own kitchen: hundreds of thousands formerly, three now. The order and the placement are the whole technique. Not a rule with an exemption, and not a rule followed quietly by its author. A rule whose author's own compliance is inscribed on the same rock, in a number anybody can hold him to.

**Scope conditions**. It works where the author's compliance is checkable and costly, and where the rule touches something the audience will resent — the resentment is what the self-inclusion is spending itself against. It fails where compliance is cheap for the author and expensive for everyone else, because then publishing it reads as a taunt. And it fails where the number cannot be verified: three creatures a day in a palace kitchen a thousand kilometres away is not, in fact, checkable, which is why the technique is stronger as rhetoric than as evidence.

**Modern equivalent:** the executive who takes the pay cut first and says the figure, versus the one who announces the freeze. Same policy, and only one of them can be argued with on the numbers.

## Ch. 9 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and this one was actually taken**. At Dhauli and Jaugada three edicts were dropped and two written specially. The default — the thing done at Girnar, at Erragudi, at Kalsi — was to publish the anthology. In the province he had destroyed, somebody decided against publishing the account of destroying it.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the thirteenth edict had gone up at Dhauli with the rest. A hundred thousand dead, told to the survivors, on a rock beside the river, read aloud by an official on the day of Tishya. It is possible to argue that this would have been the more honest course and it is not obvious it would have been the better one: the Separate Edicts that went there instead are about judges who imprison people arbitrarily, which is the grievance the province actually had that year. The forecast is that publishing the confession there buys nothing a wounded population wants, and spends the credibility needed for the thing that might have helped. **Confession travels well to people who were not the victims**. The book has him omitting it precisely where it would have been heard by them, and that is a choice about audience rather than about conscience.

## Ch. 9 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: writing one document to be read in many places you will never see**.

The pattern the chapter recovers is that fixity of medium creates an illusion of fixity of meaning. The same sentences cut on the same kind of rock in Karnataka, Gujarat, Afghanistan and Orissa were four different messages, because a message is finished by the place it lands in. At Maski it was parachuted into a landscape whose gods it did not mention, and it was ignored. At Panguraria the audience was a monastery that already agreed. At Kandahar it was translated into two languages that had no word for its central idea. In Kalinga the parts about dhamma were removed and replaced with instructions about judges.

**Scope conditions**. Local adaptation of this kind holds together only while the centre is willing to let the edges edit — and it collapses in the other direction too. Where the centre insists on literal uniformity, the message goes unread in places whose concerns it never touched; where the edges edit freely, the sender loses any idea of what was actually said in his name. The Mauryan settlement sat in the middle: identical core, local additions, local omissions, and a five-yearly inspection to check the officials rather than the text.

**Modern equivalent:** any policy issued centrally and executed in dozens of jurisdictions. The document is the same everywhere and the thing that happens is different everywhere, and the illusion that the document settles it is created by the document being the only artefact that survives.
